narrative:
The model determined that you have a 99.2% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a very high bar for admission, this strong prediction of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year in law school was the single biggest reason the model expected you to struggle on the bar. Being in the second decile—far below the average of roughly sixth decile among accepted students—strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year class rank came second; again sitting in the second decile compared with an average around the sixth decile among accepted applicants, this further increased the model’s confidence that you would not pass.

Your family’s upper-middle income bracket was the third most influential factor. While this is the most common income group among accepted students, in your specific combination of circumstances it still nudged the prediction slightly toward failure rather than success.

Taken together, these academic performance signals outweighed your LSAT score of 34, your undergraduate GPA of 2.9, and the fact that you plan to attend full-time.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or consider programs that specifically help students improve bar passage rates. Many schools offer targeted bar-prep support for students with similar profiles; reaching out to their admissions offices to discuss those resources would be a practical next step. (248 words)
